title: Neonatal Hyperglycemia -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Neonatal hyperglycemia, typically defined as serum glucose above 150 mg/dL, reflects an imbalance between glucose delivery, utilization, and insulin activity in both term and preterm infants. Contributing factors include prematurity, impaired insulin secretion, increased insulin resistance, elevated stress hormones, delayed enteral feeding, total parenteral nutrition–related metabolic effects, sepsis, medication exposures, and rare genetic syndromes. This course reviews the clinical manifestations of neonatal hyperglycemia, which are often related to underlying etiologies and may include dehydration, weight loss, temperature instability, or feeding difficulties. Accurate diagnosis with serum glucose confirmation, electrolyte monitoring, and evaluation for infection or persistent dysglycemia requiring further endocrine and genetic assessment is also discussed. Management.

title: Neonatal Hyperglycemia -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This activity examines the mechanisms of neonatal hyperglycemia and evidence-based management strategies, focusing on adjusting glucose infusion rates, addressing contributing conditions, and cautiously considering insulin therapy with close monitoring to avoid hypoglycemia. Participants will gain an in-depth knowledge of underlying causes, nutrition and glucose delivery, monitoring of metabolic stability, and safe insulin protocols. This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance the learner's competence in identifying neonatal hyperglycemia, performing the recommended evaluation, and implementing an appropriate interprofessional approach to manage this condition, thereby supporting better patient outcomes, reducing complications, and promoting safe, physiologic glucose control in at-risk infants.

title: Neonatal Hyperglycemia -- Introduction
content: Neonatal hyperglycemia is commonly defined as serum glucose greater than 150 mg/dL (8.3 mmol/L) or whole-blood glucose greater than 125 mg/dL (6.9 mmol/L), independent of gestational or postmenstrual age. A safe blood glucose target for neonates ranges from 70 to 150 mg/dL, with the upper limit set by the renal glucose threshold in preterm infants. [1] Classification depends on timing after birth: early-onset hyperglycemia occurs within the first 48 hours of life, and late-onset hyperglycemia develops after the initial 48 hours.

title: Neonatal Hyperglycemia -- Etiology
content: Prematurity and intrauterine growth restriction frequently contribute to neonatal hyperglycemia through inadequate insulin secretion and impaired suppression of hepatic glucose production. Increased insulin resistance further amplifies glucose elevation. Elevated levels of stress hormones, eg, epinephrine and norepinephrine, inhibit both insulin secretion and insulin action while simultaneously raising glucagon levels, which promote glycogenolysis. Catecholamine infusions, seizures, and physiologic stress from surgery, pain, hypoxia, respiratory distress, or sepsis commonly drive these hormonal changes.

title: Neonatal Hyperglycemia -- Etiology
content: Feeding-related factors also influence glucose regulation. A delay in initiating enteral feeding reduces incretin secretion and, subsequently, promotes hyperglycemia, while the use of hyperosmolar formulas can trigger transient glucose intolerance. [2] Total parenteral nutrition introduces additional risks. Delayed supplementation of parenteral amino acids slows the release of insulin-like growth factor-1, hindering beta-cell development and contributing to hyperglycemia. High intravenous lipid infusion rates increase free fatty acids, which competitively reduce glucose oxidation by supplying alternative substrates for oxidative metabolism; free fatty acids and glycerol further stimulate gluconeogenesis. [3]

title: Neonatal Hyperglycemia -- Etiology
content: Sepsis should be considered when hyperglycemia develops despite an unchanged glucose infusion rate, and necrotizing enterocolitis should also be assessed. Iatrogenic contributors, including errors in calculating the glucose infusion rate in intravenous fluids, frequently lead to excessive glucose delivery. Transient neonatal diabetes mellitus often affects small-for-gestational-age infants and follows a self-limited course.

title: Neonatal Hyperglycemia -- Etiology
content: Several genetic syndromes also predispose infants to hyperglycemia, including Wolcott-Rallison syndrome, DEND syndrome (Developmental delay, Epilepsy, and Neonatal Diabetes), Rogers syndrome, and IPEX syndrome (Immune dysregulation, polyendocrinopathy, enteropathy, X-linked). [4] Medication-related factors require equal attention. Maternal diazoxide exposure may cause hyperglycemia, hypotension, and tachycardia in neonates, while antenatal steroids may contribute to glucose elevation. Neonatal medications, eg, dopamine, dobutamine, epinephrine, caffeine, theophylline, phenytoin, and corticosteroids, frequently impair glucose regulation and promote hyperglycemia.

title: Neonatal Hyperglycemia -- Epidemiology
content: Hyperglycemia is more common in preterm infants than in term infants and is generally noted during the first week of life. Acute hyperglycemia usually resolves over 2 to 3 days in most neonates, but it can persist for up to 10 days. Hyperglycemia is less common than hypoglycemia among neonates, but this condition is associated with increased mortality and morbidity. Neonatal hyperglycemia is inversely related to birth weight and gestational age. [5] Hyperglycemia occurs in one-third of preterm and small for gestational age infants.

title: Neonatal Hyperglycemia -- Pathophysiology
content: Glucose is an essential energy source for the fetus and the neonate. The brain growth of the fetus exclusively depends upon glucose. In the early postnatal period, glucose homeostasis is maintained through glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. The critical regulatory mechanisms of glucose homeostasis are sluggish in the initial days, particularly among preterm neonates. [6] The mechanisms of neonatal hyperglycemia are multifactorial.

title: Neonatal Hyperglycemia -- Pathophysiology
content: The risk of hyperglycemia increases with the severity of the accompanying illness. The most common cause is high exogenous glucose infusion rates in preterm infants who are already at risk for hyperglycemia due to the following reasons: decreased ability to suppress endogenous glucose production, decreased insulin response to glucose, and limited glycogen and fat stores. [7] [6]

title: Neonatal Hyperglycemia -- History and Physical
content: No specific physical findings consistently point to hyperglycemia, although the examination may uncover indicators of an underlying condition, eg, temperature instability or low perfusion in cases of sepsis. Several nonspecific clinical features can suggest hyperglycemia, including increased urine output, dehydration, weight loss, fever, and feeding difficulty. These signs often reflect osmotic diuresis or the systemic effects of the contributing illness and warrant further evaluation to confirm elevated glucose levels and identify the precipitating cause.

title: Neonatal Hyperglycemia -- Evaluation
content: The evaluation for neonatal hyperglycemia should include careful laboratory and clinical assessments. Relying solely on point-of-care blood glucose testing may produce inaccurate results, so elevated readings should be confirmed with serum glucose measurement before initiating treatment. Venous blood glucose provides more reliable values than capillary samples, as capillary glucose from heel-stick testing tends to be approximately 15% lower and is influenced by hematocrit levels. title: Neonatal Hyperglycemia -- Evaluation
content: Urine glucose : A level of 2+ or higher suggests osmotic diuresis. Complete blood count and C-reactive protein : These studies help in ruling out sepsis. Comprehensive metabolic panel : Ongoing monitoring of serum electrolytes is critical, as osmotic diuresis can cause significant electrolyte losses. Infant weight : Tracking the infant’s weight helps assess hydration status. Insulin and C-peptide : If hyperglycemia persists beyond 2 weeks, serum insulin levels and serum and urine C-peptide levels are used to rule out monogenic diabetes and Type 1 diabetes. Genetic testing : Genetic testing should be considered if hyperglycemia continues despite prolonged insulin therapy, particularly in infants with syndromic features, a family history of diabetes, or low C-peptide levels. [8]

title: Neonatal Hyperglycemia -- Treatment / Management
content: In preterm and very-low-birth-weight infants (defined as those with a birth weight below 1500 g), persistent blood glucose levels exceeding 200 mg/dL require careful evaluation. Persistent hyperglycemia with readings above 200 mg/dL at 4-hour intervals, accompanied by glucosuria of +2 or higher, may indicate the need for treatment. Current evidence does not support treating hyperglycemia in the absence of increased osmolarity or osmotic diuresis.

title: Neonatal Hyperglycemia -- Treatment / Management -- Glucose Infusion
content: The initial step in managing neonatal hyperglycemia involves assessing the glucose infusion rate (GIR), which is calculated as the IV infusion rate (mL/kg/day) × dextrose concentration (%)/144. GIR can be reduced by decreasing either the IV dextrose concentration or the infusion rate, typically by 1 to 2 mg/kg/min every 2 hours, with frequent glucose monitoring until reaching 4 mg/kg/min. Persistent hyperglycemia warrants investigation and management of underlying causes, including sepsis, physiologic stress, and medication effects. [1]

title: Neonatal Hyperglycemia -- Treatment / Management -- Insulin Therapy
content: Insulin therapy may be indicated when hyperglycemia persists at low GIR (4 mg/kg/min), suggesting relative insulin deficiency or resistance. Insulin should be considered if blood glucose exceeds 250 mg/dL and urine glucose is +2 or higher in 2 samples taken 4 hours apart, despite GIR reduction. Bolus insulin therapy carries a high risk of hypoglycemia and is generally avoided. Continuous insulin infusion can be administered either by adding insulin to maintenance fluids or running it independently, allowing adjustment of the insulin rate without altering total IV fluid delivery.

title: Neonatal Hyperglycemia -- Treatment / Management -- Insulin Therapy
content: Initial infusion rates typically range from 0.01 to 0.05 U/kg/hour and are titrated in 0.01 U/kg/hour increments, with a maximum of 0.1 U/kg/hour. The target blood glucose range is 100 to 150 mg/dL, with gradual reductions emphasized to avoid rapid fluctuations and hypoglycemia. [9] [10] [9] Insulin infusion should be halved if glucose decreases to 180 mg/dL and discontinued if levels drop below 150 mg/dL. Rapid decreases exceeding 50 mg/dL per hour require immediate insulin adjustment or GIR increase to prevent complications (eg, cerebral edema).

title: Neonatal Hyperglycemia -- Treatment / Management -- Insulin Therapy
content: Hourly glucose monitoring during insulin therapy is essential, with rechecks 30 minutes after any infusion change. Hypoglycemia requires discontinuation of insulin and administration of 2 mL/kg D10 IV bolus, followed by monitoring for rebound hyperglycemia. Recent case reports suggest subcutaneous insulin glargine may provide a safer and more stable alternative to intravenous infusion in selected neonates, although standardized protocols remain limited. [11] [12] Correcting electrolyte imbalances caused by osmotic diuresis, particularly sodium and potassium disturbances, is critical.

title: Neonatal Hyperglycemia -- Treatment / Management -- Preventative Measures
content: Prevention of hyperglycemia is essential in all neonates, especially preterm infants, due to increased risks of infection, impaired immunity, poor wound healing, and higher morbidity and mortality. Preventive strategies include early initiation of enteral feeding, timely amino acid supplementation in TPN to stimulate insulin secretion, targeting physiologic GIR based on glucose monitoring, and limiting IV lipid infusions during hyperglycemia. Direct interventions, such as reducing or discontinuing catecholamine infusions and glucocorticoid therapy as soon as clinically feasible, further support glucose stabilization and overall metabolic health.

title: Neonatal Hyperglycemia -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Neonatal hyperglycemia typically reflects an underlying clinical condition rather than a primary disorder of glucose metabolism. It may signal serious illnesses such as sepsis, necrotizing enterocolitis, or seizures. A rare cause of neonatal hyperglycemia is neonatal diabetes mellitus, which occurs in approximately 1 in 400,000 births. [13] Neonatal diabetes presents in the following 3 distinct forms: The transient form accounts for more than 50% of cases and is often caused by mutations in sulfonylurea receptors. This form typically manifests shortly after birth and resolves spontaneously within 6 months. Permanent neonatal diabetes needs lifelong management. Mutations in the genes encoding the subunit of the ATP-sensitive potassium channel are the most common cause. [8] Syndromic neonatal diabetes is usually associated with syndromes like Wolfram syndrome and IPEX syndrome (immune dysregulation polyendocrinopathy X-linked syndrome).

title: Neonatal Hyperglycemia -- Prognosis
content: Neonatal hyperglycemia, particularly in preterm neonates, is usually associated with an increased risk of mortality and morbidity. The severity of impact increases with prolonged hyperglycemia. Prompt evaluation and management of neonatal hyperglycemia decrease the impact.

title: Neonatal Hyperglycemia -- Complications
content: Hyperglycemia in preterm and very-low-birth-weight infants significantly increases both mortality and morbidity, with prolonged hyperglycemia contributing to more severe outcomes. Affected neonates face elevated risks of multiple complications. Intracranial hemorrhage may result from hyperosmolarity and osmotic fluid shifts, with each increment of 18 mg/dL in blood glucose raising serum osmolarity by 1 mOsm/L. [14] Serum osmolarity exceeding 300 mOsm/L can trigger rapid water shifts, increasing the risk of cerebral hemorrhage. Osmotic diuresis leads to dehydration and electrolyte imbalances, with glycosuria further promoting sodium loss.

title: Neonatal Hyperglycemia -- Complications
content: Hyperglycemia has also been linked to necrotizing enterocolitis, although study findings vary, and its association with retinopathy of prematurity remains inconsistent, despite experimental models suggesting impaired retinal angiogenesis. For instance, Soghier et al and Kao et al demonstrated a significant association between hyperglycemia and necrotizing enterocolitis, whereas Akmal et al reported no significant association. [15] [16] Sustained hyperglycemia in the neonatal mouse model has been associated with impaired retinal angiogenesis, similar to that observed in retinopathy of prematurity. However, clinical evidence in humans is inconsistent. While some studies suggest an association between hyperglycemia and retinopathy of prematurity, a meta-analysis of 9 studies involving 1,939 infants found no significant association between mean blood glucose levels and the development of ROP. [17] [18] [19] [20]

title: Neonatal Hyperglycemia -- Complications
content: Dysregulated glucose metabolism may contribute to bronchopulmonary dysplasia by increasing oxidative stress and impairing alveolar growth, while hyperglycemia can compromise immunity and elevate the risk of late-onset sepsis. [21] Hyperglycemia was significantly associated with an increased incidence of late-onset sepsis, consistent with findings by Ramel et al, [22] and Van der Lugt et al. [23] However, Sabzehei et al. [24] reported no significant association. Sepsis itself may contribute to hyperglycemia by enhancing stress response, reducing insulin secretion, and impairing peripheral glucose utilization. Poor wound healing and long-term effects, including insulin resistance, glucose intolerance, and adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes, have also been reported. [25] [26] [27]

title: Neonatal Hyperglycemia -- Complications
content: Management of neonatal hyperglycemia carries additional risks. Insulin infusion may induce hypoglycemia and hypokalemia, emphasizing the importance of addressing underlying causes alongside glucose control. While hyperglycemia may directly have adverse effects, the evidence is unclear as to whether the underlying condition (eg, infection) or the higher glucose levels themselves are the primary drivers of many of the adverse outcomes identified above.

title: Neonatal Hyperglycemia -- Complications
content: For example, several studies have found an association of hyperglycemia with various adverse outcomes in preterm neonates, such as intraventricular hemorrhage, Necrotizing enterocolitis, retinopathy of prematurity, fungal infections, prolonged hospitalization, and mortality. [28] [25] Titchiner et al, in a large multicenter cohort study, observed that premature infants with hyperglycemia who received insulin treatment for more than 14 days had a significantly increased risk of retinopathy of prematurity and chronic lung disease. [29]

title: Neonatal Hyperglycemia -- Complications
content: A randomized controlled trial and its long-term follow-up found that tight glycemic control in hyperglycemic preterm infants improved early growth but increased the incidence of hypoglycemia, with no long-term neurodevelopmental benefits observed at school age. [30] A Cochrane review concluded that evidence is insufficient to determine whether insulin treatment or reducing GIR improves outcomes in hyperglycemic very low birth weight infants, highlighting the need for further research. [31]

title: Neonatal Hyperglycemia -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Deterrence of neonatal hyperglycemia centers on anticipatory management and proactive education for all caregivers involved in the infant’s care. Early initiation of enteral feeding, timely supplementation of amino acids in TPN, and careful titration of glucose and lipid infusion rates help maintain physiologic glucose balance, particularly in preterm infants. Clinicians should emphasize the importance of minimizing unnecessary catecholamine or corticosteroid use and discontinuing these agents as soon as the infant stabilizes. By reinforcing evidence-based monitoring practices and accurate GIR calculations, the healthcare team can reduce preventable episodes of dysglycemia and associated complications, eg, dehydration, electrolyte imbalances, and increased morbidity.

title: Neonatal Hyperglycemia -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Patient and family education focuses on explaining the factors influencing glucose control, the rationale for frequent glucose and electrolyte monitoring, and the steps taken to adjust nutrition and medications to support metabolic stability. Clear communication about the potential signs of infection, feeding intolerance, or worsening hydration allows families to participate in early recognition of clinical changes. Engaging parents in discussions about the neonatal course fosters understanding, reduces anxiety, and strengthens collaborative care, ultimately supporting safer, more effective management throughout the infant’s hospitalization.

Engaging parents in discussions about the neonatal course fosters understanding, reduces anxiety, and strengthens collaborative care, ultimately supporting safer, more effective management throughout the infant’s hospitalization.

title: Neonatal Hyperglycemia -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Neonatal hyperglycemia, defined as serum glucose above 150 mg/dL, reflects an imbalance between glucose delivery, utilization, and insulin activity, particularly in preterm and very low birth weight infants. Contributing factors include inadequate insulin secretion, increased insulin resistance, elevated stress hormones, delayed enteral feeding, TPN-related metabolic effects, sepsis, medication exposure, and uncommon genetic syndromes. Clinical signs often stem from underlying etiologies, and accurate diagnosis requires serum glucose confirmation, electrolyte evaluation, and targeted workup for infection or persistent dysglycemia. Management centers on adjusting the glucose infusion rate, addressing contributing conditions, and cautiously introducing insulin therapy with close monitoring to avoid hypoglycemia.

title: Neonatal Hyperglycemia -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: High-quality, patient-centered care relies on coordinated efforts across the healthcare team. Physicians, general practitioners, and advanced practitioners must accurately assess metabolic status, interpret laboratory data, individualize GIR adjustments, and determine when insulin therapy is appropriate. Nurses support continuous monitoring, recognize early changes in hydration or glucose trends, and ensure timely communication of abnormalities. Pharmacists optimize TPN composition, guide safe insulin preparation, and evaluate drug-related contributors. Dietitians, genetic counselors, and laboratory professionals contribute to nutritional planning and targeted diagnostic evaluation. Clear interprofessional communication, shared decision-making, and structured care pathways strengthen safety, promote physiologic glucose control, and improve outcomes for vulnerable neonates.
